Operator Station Lockout/Tagout Procedure Reference: The documented LOTO steps are: 1) At the operator station HMI, navigate to the 'Visu_Dual_MCP' screen. 2) Press CYCLE STOP. 3) If carriage movement is needed, press JOG, select the corresponding tipper axis, and use the + and – buttons.

OptiSweep Tipper Operation: QR codes on the floor direct the AGV with the tote to an open tipper. When the gripper on the tipper senses the tote, it pulls the tote onto the tipper, which deposits the parcel into a parcel bag via a chute. A bag ID label is generated and placed on the bag by the bagging employee.

Operator Station Overview: The operator station is a defined area within the OptiSweep system where an operator receives parcels from the tippers. It contains two tippers, a chute, plastic curtains, a rotary station, an HMI screen, and four push-buttons. Two stacklights are mounted on the top of the frame on either side of the chute.

Operator Station Components: The operator station features are identified in Table 3-1 and Figure 3-1. The components are: 1. Tipper, 2. Chute, 3. Stacklight, 4. Plastic curtain, 5. Operator station HMI, 6. Push-buttons, 7. Rotary station.
Operator Station HMI: The operator station includes an HMI screen as one of its components, as listed in Table 3-1 and shown in Figure 3-1.
Operator Station Stacklights: Two stacklights are mounted on the top of the frame on either side of the chute at the operator station.

Operator Station Push-Button Descriptions: Item 1: Starts the left tipper cycle. Item 2: Starts the left tipper cycle for a Surepost tote. Item 3: Starts the right tipper cycle for a Surepost tote. Item 4: Starts the right tipper cycle. Item 5: Emergency stop push-button.
OptiSweep HMI Interfaces: The three HMI interfaces are: System API, Operator station HMI, and Hospital HMI. The manual details screens associated with each interface in subsequent sections.

OptiSweep HMI Interfaces Overview: The System HMI ties into the existing customer system. The Operator Station HMI and Hospital HMI are separate panels. Each interface has associated screens detailed in the manual.
Operator Station HMI Screen Location: The HMI screen is physically located on the right side of each tipper station. It is used to set parameters and control the tippers.

Operator Station HMI Navigation Methods: Screens can be navigated in three ways: the Next Screen drop-down menu, buttons on the right side of the screen, and buttons on the right side of the physical display. The physical buttons navigate to the same screen as the corresponding on-screen button.

Operator Station Primary Screens: Station operators will only need to use the main control panel screen (F3 button), the data screen (F5 button), and the alarms screen (F6 button). The F3 button navigates to the 'Visu_MCP_Dual' screen, which is the primary screen operators need to use.

Operator Station Function Key Screen Mapping: The function keys map to the following screens: F1 navigates to 'Visu_ManControl', F2 navigates to 'Visu_MDs', F3 navigates to 'Visu_MCP_Dual', F4 navigates to 'Visu_IO_Diag', F5 navigates to 'Visu_Data', and F6 navigates to 'Visu_Alarm'.

Operator Station Selection and Navigation Controls: Use the arrow buttons to navigate to items on the screen. Press the center button to select the item navigated to on the screen. A drop-down menu also provides direct selection of the next screen to view.
Visu_MCP_Dual AUTO Button: Item 2 in the control panel description. Pressing AUTO is required to restart the system after an E-stop reset.
Visu_MCP_Dual Fault and E-Stop Reset Sequence: Items 7 and 9 in the control panel description. The AUTO REF button (item 8) is enabled after pressing RESET.

VISU_DATA Screen Overview: The VISU_DATA screen is described in section 4.1.2.2 of the OptiSweep Operation and Maintenance Manual. It is the primary monitoring interface for the operator station, consolidating several key performance indicator (KPI) sections: Tipper Stats, Process Status, RunTime Meters, Operator Stats, and Heartbeat Stats.

VISU_MANCONTROL Screen Overview: This screen is part of the Operator Station HMI. It includes an informational banner for alarms/messages, displays the currently logged-in user ID, and provides manual control buttons for system components like tippers and grippers.

LEFT/RIGHT TIPPER FAULT RESET Button: These are manual control buttons on the Operator Station HMI. They are specific to the left and right tippers and are used to clear a fault condition on the selected tipper.

LEFT/RIGHT TIPPER DISABLE Button: These are manual control buttons on the Operator Station HMI for disabling the left or right tipper. The system provides visual feedback for this state via the stacklight turning solid blue.

wCommand Screen: This screen is used for diagnosing communication between the Operator Station and the Warehouse Control System (WCS). It shows the current command words being exchanged, providing insight into the WCS-Operator Station interface for each tipper.

VISU_IO_DIAG Screen Overview: This screen is part of the Operator Station HMI. It is explicitly noted as read-only and intended for troubleshooting purposes. It includes an informational banner for alarms/messages, temperature readings for the CPU and motherboard, voltage readings for the internal controller, and statuses for station switches and...

VISU_ALARM Screen: The Visu_Alarm screen is part of the Operator Station HMI. It provides a list of all tipper alarms, each accompanied by a timestamp. The screen includes a SHOW HISTORY button that, when activated, displays the last 1500 alarm records.

Tipper Alarms on Operator Station HMI: The Operator Station HMI includes a dedicated screen, Visu_Alarm, for monitoring tipper alarms. Each alarm event is listed with its associated timestamp, allowing operators to track the sequence and timing of tipper faults.

Tipper Cycle Stop Alarm: For both the Left and Right Tippers, alarm ID 13 ('Tipper Cycle Stopped') is triggered when the operator station enters a Cycle Stopped state. The controller response is that the cycle stops. The corrective action is to press CYCLE START to resume or RESET to end the cycle.

Operator Station Startup Prerequisites: The startup procedure requires two preconditions: 1) AGVs must be powered on (refer to P40A V2.0 user manual for AGV startup instructions), and 2) the main disconnect must be in the ON position.

Operator Station E-Stop Reset: During operator station startup, a flashing ESTOP indicates a fault condition. The operator must physically pull out the ESTOP button and then press the RESET button on the HMI screen to clear the fault state before proceeding.

Operator Station Shutdown (CYCLE STOP): The operator station is stopped by pressing the CYCLE STOP button located on the operator station main screen. This is distinct from the system-level shutdown procedure described in section 5.2.

Operator Station Stop Procedure: The documented step to stop the operator station is a single action: pressing the CYCLE STOP button on the operator station main screen. This is distinct from the system shutdown procedure, which is initiated from the system HMI API screen.

Operator Station Startup Procedure: The startup procedure for the operator station includes: 1) Verifying AGVs are powered on. 2) Verifying the main disconnect is ON. 3) At the operator station control panel, if the E-STOP is flashing, pulling out the E-STOP and pressing RESET on the HMI to clear faults.

Operator Station HMI CYCLE STOP Button: The operator station main screen includes a CYCLE STOP button. This button is the primary control for stopping the operator station, as per the documented procedure. An image of this screen is available in the manual.

Tipper Jogging Mode: Jogging mode allows manual positioning of the left and right tipper end effectors. It is accessed from the 'Visu_Dual_MCP' screen (F3) on the operator station HMI. The automatic tipping cycle must be stopped by pressing CYCLE STOP before jogging is enabled. Pressing JOG opens the jogging screen.

HMI MCP_Dual Screen (F3): The 'MCP_Dual' screen is a specific HMI screen on the operator station. It is referenced in the context of stopping a tipping cycle during a non-recoverable motor fault recovery process.

HMI CYCLE STOP Control: The CYCLE STOP control is a button on the operator station HMI, specifically mentioned in the context of the 'MCP_Dual' screen. Its function is to stop the tipping cycle, which is a required step when recovering from a non-recoverable motor fault on a tipper.

MCP_Dual Screen (F3): The MCP_Dual screen is accessed by navigating to F3 on the operator station HMI. It is used during non-recoverable fault recovery processes. The screen displays axis statuses for Z1, Z2, A1, and A2, and includes buttons for CYCLE STOP, JOG, RESET, AUTO, and CYCLE START.

Operator Station Axes (Z1, Z2, A1, A2): During a non-recoverable fault recovery, if a tote is lifted off the robot, the operator can jog the Z-axis or A-axis to position the tote on or nearly on the robot. The manual specifies that A1 and Z1 are used for the left axis, and A2 and Z2 are used for the right tipper.

Hospital Station: During the final steps of a non-recoverable fault recovery for operator station motors, after pressing AUTO and CYCLE START, the grippers release and the robot is commanded to go to the hospital station. The operator must press RESET after the robot has left the tipper.

Non-Recoverable Fault: AGV Stuck: This fault is verified on the operator station HMI. The OUT Fault Status for the affected tipper should have a value of 82. Recovery involves forcing a value on OUT W1: a value of 3 if the tote and AGV are ready to continue, or 32771 if the AGV needs to go to the hospital.

HMI Screen: Visu_ManControl: The 'Visu_ManControl' screen contains a 'CellIO Status' button. This screen is part of the operator station HMI and is used during the recovery procedure for a non-recoverable AGV stuck fault.

Required Information Before Entering the Dance Floor: The manual specifies that before going inside the grid (a.k.a. the Dance Floor), the following information is required: Robot ID, Fault description from RMS, whether RMS thinks the faulted AGV is holding a bin (and the tote ID if so), and if the faulted AGV is under a rack, whether that AGV is the empty AGV for that...

RMS E-Stop: The manual describes using an E-stop for the RMS as part of the bump fault recovery process. The steps include 'E-stop the RMS' and later 'Press E-stop again', implying a toggle or release action.

Add AGV to Zone with No Empty AGV Procedure Reference: This procedure is used when a zone lacks an empty AGV. Steps include: 1) E-stop RMS. 2) Move an AGV into the zone under the tote rack. 3) Add AGV in RMS using Tote API Controls. 4) Wait for AGV to turn blue. 5) Verify AGV status is 'szonestaging' on the HMI. If the AGV is moving to the Hospital, remove and re-add it.

AGVS Lost Tasks Recovery Procedure Reference: This procedure addresses the scenario where empty AGVs have lost their tasks due to an RMS restart. Steps include: 1) E-stop RMS. 2) Remove and re-add AGVs without totes twice using Tote API Controls. 3) If the system needs to be restarted, ensure AGVs are in the 'szonestaging' state (verified on HMI).

Add AGV to Zone with No Empty AGV Screen: This screen, shown in Figure 5-3, is part of the 'Add AGV to Zone with No Empty AGV' fault recovery procedure. The operator must E-stop the RMS, physically move an AGV into the zone under the tote rack, and then use this screen to add the AGV.

Faulted AGV with Tote Recovery Concept: The recovery concept for a 'Faulted AGV with Tote' involves a sequence of actions: E-stop the RMS, remove the AGV from the RMS, take the tote to the Hospital and remove the AGV via the Hospital HMI, add the AGV back into the RMS, press the E-Stop again, and resume the RMS.

AGV Fault During Exchange Recovery Concept: For an 'AGV Fault During Exchange', the described concept is to E-stop the RMS, remove the faulted AGV that is lifted. If the AGV behind it does not backfill, that AGV should also be removed. The final step is to introduce a new tote at that location and place an empty AGV in that zone.

AGV Lost Tote (No Fault) Recovery Concept: The recovery concept for 'AGV Lost Tote No Fault' includes: E-stop the RMS, press the brake release on the AGV, push the AGV to the Hospital, remove and re-add the AGV at the Hospital station PC, power cycle the AGV, roll it over a QR code when lights are green, locate the missing tote and bring it to the Hospital for...

E-Stop Zone Reset Procedure: This procedure is referenced in multiple troubleshooting entries for 'Obstruction/parcel on floor' and 'AGV motionless on floor'. The steps are: 1. Reference E-stop zone map. Press E-STOP to stop the appropriate E-stop zone. 2. Remove the parcel/debris or faulted AGV. 3. Pull E-STOP. 4. Press the blue RESET button. 5.

Operator Station Daily Preventive Maintenance: The operator station is a component of the OptiSweep system. Daily preventive maintenance tasks are: 1) Inspect the controller for damage. 2) Verify stacklights are operational. 3) Ensure the chute is free of debris (e.g., stuck labels).

Daily Preventive Maintenance for Operator Station: The operator station must be inspected daily for: damage to the controller, operational stacklights, and a chute free of debris (e.g., stuck labels).

Operator Station Daily Preventive Maintenance Inspection: The operator station is part of the daily preventive maintenance routine. The inspection checklist includes: (1) checking the controller for any damage, (2) confirming that the stacklights are operational, and (3) ensuring the chute is free of debris, specifically noting stuck labels as an example.

Daily Maintenance Checklist: The checklist includes the following tasks: Inspect the Operator Station controller for damage; Ensure Operator Station chute is free of debris; Verify stacklights are operational; Inspect the guards and verify attaching hardware is secure; Inspect all QR codes on the floor for damage or peeling; Inspect all QR codes...

Manual Axes Referencing Initiation: To manually reference axes, navigate to the 'Visu_Dual_MCP' screen (F3) on the operator station HMI and press CYCLE STOP to stop the automatic tipping cycle. This allows manual positioning of the end effector.

Tipper Replacement Prerequisites: Before removing the tipper, LOTO must be applied to the tipper (referencing Operator Station Lockout/Tagout procedure on page 2). Required PPE includes safety glasses and gloves. The procedure recommends optionally removing the gripper (page 97) and counter-balance weights (page 95) to facilitate the replacement.

Set Tipper Controller Parameters: Setting controller parameters is step 2 of tipper commissioning. The operator must navigate to the 'Visu_MDs' screen (F2) on the operator station HMI. Access to change settings requires logging in as maintenance or admin.

HMI Screen: Visu_MDs (F2): The 'Visu_MDs' screen is an HMI screen on the operator station. It is accessed by pressing F2. Its documented use is for setting initial parameters for each axis of the tippers. Changing settings on this screen requires maintenance or admin level login.

Tipper station overview at operator stations: The source states that each operator station has two tippers. An incoming load from an AGV is clamped by the tipper, the tipping arm actuates to dump contents onto the chute, and the tote is then placed back onto the AGV. The slide presents this as a Fortna R&D design concept for the station.

Safety Signal Words and Symbols: DANGER indicates a hazardous situation that will result in death or serious injury. WARNING indicates a hazardous situation that could result in death or serious injury. CAUTION indicates a hazardous situation that could result in minor or moderate injury.
Operator Safety Responsibility: A carelessly and improperly operated conveyor can cause serious injury, death, or equipment damage. FORTNA Inc. is not responsible for injuries or equipment damage.

Lift Connecting Rod Assembly Safety Warning: This warning applies when the robot is powered on. The operator is responsible for verifying the area around the lift connecting rod assembly is clear before initiating robot operation. Failure to follow these instructions can result in death, serious injury, or equipment damage.

Robot Movement Trajectory Safety Warning: This is a general safety warning for anyone near the operating equipment. Interference with the movement trajectory can result in death, serious injury, or equipment damage.
Tipper Overview: The tipper is a component that interfaces with AGVs to receive totes. When the gripper senses a tote, it pulls the tote up the tipper and empties the parcels into a chute.

Tipper Components: The tipper components are identified in Figure 3-4 and Table 3-3. Components include: 1) Upper hard stops, 2) Z-axis motor, 3) Z-axis cable carrier, 4) A-axis motor, 5) Lower hard stops, 6) CLINK controller cover, 7) Column, 8) Sub-plate, 9) Counterbalances, 10) Counterbalance carriage, 11) Timing belt, 12) A-axis...

Tipper Gripper Operation: The gripper is the component that interfaces directly with the tote. It senses the presence of the tote and initiates the action of pulling the tote up the tipper, which results in the parcels being emptied into a chute.

AGV Brake Release: The manual mentions an AGV brake release in the context of recovering an AGV that has lost a tote. The operator is instructed to press the brake release on the AGV to then push it over to the Hospital.

Maintenance References for P40 Robots and Tipper: The OptiSweep system includes P40 (V2.0) robots and a tipper. Maintenance procedures for the robots are documented in the P40A (V2.0) user manual, Document version V1.1 (20231206). Maintenance for the tipper is handled by Lifecycle Performance Services (LPS), reachable at 888-444-4647.

Tipper Preventive Maintenance Schedule: Once the system is live, tipper inspections must be done weekly for the first four weeks. Then, inspections must occur monthly for four months. Then, inspections must occur every 6 months going forward. The Tipper Inspection Checklist on page 209 should be used during inspections.
Tipper Inspection Checklist Reference: The manual references a Tipper Inspection Checklist located on page 209. This checklist should be used during inspections to avoid missing important tasks.

Tipper Preventive Maintenance Inspection Schedule: Once the system is live, tipper inspections must be done weekly for the first four weeks, then monthly for four months, and then every 6 months going forward. A Tipper Inspection Checklist (page 209) should be used during inspections.

Tipper Re-commissioning Requirement After Part Replacement: The manual states that a tipper needs to be re-commissioned after any part is replaced. No further details on the re-commissioning procedure are provided in this section.

Stacklight Replacement Overview: The stacklight is a three-segment assembly. Replacement involves disconnecting an M12 connector. Required PPE includes safety glasses and gloves. The procedure is estimated to take 30 minutes.
Stacklight M12 Connector: The stacklight is connected via an M12 connector. Disconnecting this connector is the first step in the removal procedure.

Tipper Replacement Overview: The tipper is mounted to a sub-plate with four hex head screws. It has connections for power (6-pin Molex), Ethernet (to ClearLink controller), and an air line with a quick disconnect at the bottom of the column. A side panel provides access to the motor.

Tipper Connections: The power cable uses a 6-pin Molex connector. The Ethernet cable connects to the ClearLink controller. The air line has a quick disconnect located at the bottom of the column; during removal, the quick disconnect is left on the tipper side. All three connections are routed through a conduit to the column.

Tipper Mounting: The tipper mounts onto an existing sub-plate. Four hex head screws hold the tipper to the sub-plate. A side panel secured by nine self-tapping screws can be removed with a 3/8-inch wrench or socket to access the motor.

Tipper Commissioning Overview: The tipper commissioning process is required after any tipper component replacement. The goal is to align the replaced tipper with the other tipper, ensuring grippers and axes are level. The process requires two people, three hours, and tools including a level, digital measure, large square, and screwdriver.

Tipper Commissioning Tools and Personnel Requirements: The documented requirements for performing tipper commissioning are: two personnel, an estimated time of three hours, and tools including a level, digital measure, large square, and screwdriver.
Apply Power to Tipper Station: The first step in tipper commissioning is applying power. This is done by turning the power switch on the electrical panel to the 'On' position.

Scanner Replacement Setup Procedure: The setup procedure requires a Windows 10 or 11 laptop with 'Barcode Interface.exe' installed, a Zebra DS3608-SR scanner dock with USB cable and power adapter, two 120 VAC outlets, and network connectivity from the laptop to the AGV and Hospital control (validated by ping).

Barcode Interface Application: The application is identified by a FORTNA logo on the desktop. It provides connectivity status (green/red indicator) and a 'Calibrate Scanner' function for troubleshooting.

Scanner Setup Network Connectivity Requirements: The laptop used for scanner setup must be able to reach the AGV and Hospital control over the network. This is a prerequisite validated by a ping command. The Barcode Interface application also provides a visual connectivity status (green for good, red for bad) on the bottom right of its screen.

Scanner Setup Hardware Requirements: The setup uses a Zebra DS3608-SR scanner dock. The connection procedure involves connecting the RJ45 side of the USB cable to the back of the dock, the USB end to the laptop, and the auxiliary power connector to the power adapter, which must be plugged into a 120 VAC outlet. The dock should light up when powered.

Side fins for package centering: The speaker explains that the tote rack has fins on the side that help move packages toward the center if they hit. This describes a passive mechanical centering feature intended to reduce off-center package placement within the tote.

Tipper mechanical handling functions: The source identifies several stable functions of the tipper assembly: it clamps the tote arriving from the AGV, uses actuators to tip the arm, dumps the tote contents onto the chute, and places the tote back onto the AGV.

Brake lock behavior during robot restart cycle: According to the transcript, after a physical or remote restart, the operator must wait until the robot turns green before moving it because the brakes stay locked.
